one_liner: Experimental Arm64/macOS WebAssembly JIT with a fused validate-and-compile pass; starts big modules about 3x faster than Wasmtime.
what_it_does: A WebAssembly runtime for Apple Silicon Macs that validates and compiles a module to Arm64 machine code in one pass, then runs it with a built-in WASI preview1 layer. The C++ API is Module::compile<Mac, arm64::Arm64>(bytes), mod->instantiate(imports), and externalize<void()>() to call an export; host functions are bound with internalize<f>(). It is a research project ('Not meant for production use'), not a drop-in for Wasmtime's API or CLI.
how_it_is_fast: Startup: validation and code generation happen in one linear pass per function (validate_and_compile), with no IR and no optimizer, which is why it beats Wasmtime's Cranelift compile on large binaries. The current 'baseline' backend is a single-pass compiler whose validation stack also tracks where each value lives (register, stack slot, immediate or condition flags): locals live in callee-saved registers, temporaries come from an LRU register cache, constants fold into immediates, and comparisons stay in flags until a branch consumes them. Bounds checks are removed by reserving 16 GiB of PROT_NONE address space per linear memory (guard regions on both sides, mprotect to grow), and stack overflow is caught by a guard page instead of per-push checks. The older 'minimal' backend emits a chain of calls into precompiled C++ handlers ([[clang::musttail]], preserve_most on cold trap paths), an unrolled interpreter.
when_to_use: Research or teaching: a compact, readable single-pass Wasm-to-Arm64 compiler (register cache, flag tracking, guard-page bounds checks) to study or borrow ideas from.
Short-lived runs of very large Wasm binaries on an Apple Silicon Mac where compile latency dominates (author's numbers: SpiderMonkey starts in 65.8 ms vs 183.3 ms for Wasmtime).
Comparing baseline-compiler design choices against Wasmtime Winch or Cranelift on the same Arm64 machine.
when_not_to_use: Anything shipped: no LICENSE file (all rights reserved by default), README says 'Not meant for production use', no build file in the repo.
Linux, Windows or x86-64: the pager uses MAP_JIT, pthread_jit_write_protect_np and SIGBUS from macOS; backend/current.hpp errors out on x86.
Peak-throughput workloads: the single-pass backend loses to Wasmtime on Coremark (26616 vs 28260) and the SpiderMonkey score (347 vs 577); only esbuild was faster (3.126 s vs 3.316 s, 1.06x).
Modules that use SIMD (v128 is commented out in spec.hpp), threads or multiple concurrent instances/threads (one process-wide value stack and trap jmp_buf).
Multi-tenant or embedding hosts: it installs process-wide SIGBUS and SIGILL handlers and reserves 16 GiB of address space per memory plus 400 bytes of executable space per code-section byte.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the macOS SDK (libkern/OSCacheControl.h, pthread JIT write protection); the test harness needs wast2json from WABT and Python 3
integration.min_toolchain: Clang with C++20 (uses [[clang::musttail]], preserve_most, std::ranges, std::bit_cast); no Makefile or CMake file is committed, so flags are not documented
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: Instance::initial_stack is one process-global 5 MB value stack, runtime::trap_buf is a global jmp_buf, and the heap registry used by the SIGBUS handler is a global vector.

gotchas: Code-reading finding: the shipped main.cpp and test/executor.cpp both include backend/arm64/baseline.hpp, and nothing includes the minimal backend (minimal.cpp, backend/minimal/composer.hpp); backend/current.hpp includes a non-existent ./arm64.hpp. The post's 'unrolled JIT' numbers are therefore not reproducible from HEAD without restoring an older wiring.

Branch-range checks are assert()-only and twice too loose: bcond/cbz/cbnz accept byte offsets below 2 MiB although the 19-bit field reaches only +-1 MiB (b/bl accept 256 MiB vs a +-128 MiB range), and a release build with NDEBUG drops them, so a branch that is out of range would silently wrap. The minimal backend's put_br encodes stack offsets in a 9-bit field with only a comment ('should be handled better when src/dst are higher than 1<<9'). Not observed failing; it bites only very large functions or deep value stacks.

Trap handling is longjmp out of signal handlers (SIGBUS for guard regions, SIGILL for encoded trap instructions); the handlers are installed process-wide, and the heap registry never removes freed memories, so a later SIGBUS in a reused address range could be taken for a Wasm trap.

The JIT region is reserved as 400 bytes per code-section byte plus 400 per function, and its size is stored in a uint32_t header, so code sections above about 10.7 MB unmap only part of the region on free; the instruction cache is never invalidated after writing code (sys_icache_invalidate is commented out; the source comment reasons fresh pages cannot hold stale lines).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Wasmi or wasm3 only to study an Arm64 single-pass JIT design, since those are portable, licensed and maintained interpreters with near-zero startup; pick WAMR or Wasmtime itself for anything that must ship. Against wisp (another baseline compiler compared with Winch and Singlepass), mitey-jit's distinctive part is guard-page bounds checks and flag/register tracking during validation on Arm64.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own blog post (csjh.blog, unreachable here; numbers relayed by search snippets) timed load+validate+instantiate with hyperfine on an M1 MacBook Air: SpiderMonkey 52.8 ms (unrolled JIT) and 65.8 ms (single-pass JIT) vs Wasmtime 183.3 ms, Wasmtime single-pass 197.4 ms and Node 66.3 ms; Figma 159.7 / 198.8 ms vs Wasmtime 710.4 ms and Node 92.5 ms. Execution (median of three): the single-pass JIT ran esbuild in 3.126 s vs Wasmtime 3.316 s and Node 3.694 s but lost to Wasmtime on Coremark and SpiderMonkey; compiler flags, Wasmtime and Node versions and Wasmtime cache settings are not known.
